title: Relative slices and their coherent sections
statement: Use the universes, smallness, compactness and filteredness of [def-coef-presentable-infinity-category] and the coherent functors, mapping spaces and colimits of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Use cocartesian fibrations from [def-coef-infinity-fibrations]; for an arbitrary simplicial base use the same inner-horn and cocartesian-edge lifting conditions. Let $\mathcal C$ be a locally small quasicategory, let $D\subseteq\mathcal C$ be a replete full subcategory, let $K$ be a small simplicial set, and let $p:K\to\mathcal C$ be a diagram. Form the simplicial pullback $E=K\times_{p,\mathcal C,\operatorname{ev}_1}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,\mathcal C)$ and retain those simplices whose source vertices lie in $D$; call the resulting simplicial set $E_D$. The projection $E_D\to K$ is a cocartesian fibration. Its fiber at $v$ is the coherent slice $D_{/p(v)}$, and transport over an edge $e:v\to w$ is postcomposition by $p(e)$. The quasicategory of all sections $\operatorname{Fun}_{/K}(K,E_D)$ is equivalent to the coherent comma category of pairs $(d,\alpha)$ with $d:K\to D$ and $\alpha:d\to p$ a coherent transformation in $\operatorname{Fun}(K,\mathcal C)$, including its higher simplices. If $D$ is essentially small, this section category and $\operatorname{Fun}(K,D)$ are essentially small. For every $x\in\mathcal C$, the source functor $\mathcal C_{/x}\to\mathcal C$ creates every colimit whose underlying source diagram has a colimit in $\mathcal C$. If a class of diagram shapes has colimits in $\mathcal C$ and $D$ is closed under these colimits in $\mathcal C$, then the corresponding colimits exist in $D_{/x}$, are computed on sources, and postcomposition $D_{/x}\to D_{/y}$ preserves them for every arrow $x\to y$.

source.place: Corollary 2.4.7.11 and the dual of Corollary 2.4.7.12 (arrow fibrations), Proposition 4.2.2.4 and the relative-slice construction in the proof of Proposition 5.4.4.3; Proposition 1.2.13.8 (colimits in overcategories). The essential-smallness assertion uses a small representative of D and the small mapping spaces into p. Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this coherent result.

proof.text: Put $A_D=\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,\mathcal C)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_0,\mathcal C}D$, with target projection $q:A_D\to\mathcal C$. It is the full subcategory of the arrow quasicategory on arrows with source in $D$. Target evaluation is an inner fibration by the restriction/isofibration theorem with $\{1\}\subset\Delta^1$. Its restriction to $A_D$ is still an inner fibration: in any inner-horn problem all source vertices of a filler already belong to $D$, so fullness retains the filler. Given $a:d\to x$ and $u:x\to y$, fill the composition horn to obtain $b:d\to y$ and its composition triangle. This triangle, together with the degenerate triangle at $d$, is a square, hence an edge $s:a\to b$ of $A_D$ over $u$ whose source component is $1_d$. To verify cocartesianness, fix $c:z\to t$ in $A_D$ and write $P=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(d,z)$, $Q=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(d,t)$. The arrow-morphism formula identifies $\operatorname{Map}_{A_D}(b,c)$ with $P\times_Q^h\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(y,t)$ and $\operatorname{Map}_{A_D}(a,c)$ with $P\times_Q^h\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(x,t)$. The maps to $Q$ are composition with $c$ and with $b$, respectively with $a$; the chosen triangle identifies the latter after precomposition by $u$. Thus the mapping square for $s$ is the base-change square of these two pullbacks (a point on either iterated pullback is the same triple and its compatibility path). It is a homotopy pullback. The cocartesian mapping criterion makes $s$ horn-cocartesian. This constructs all required lifts and proves that $q$ is a cocartesian fibration.

source.place: Agent reconstruction of the cocartesian dual of Corollary 2.4.7.12, using the mapping criterion of Proposition 2.4.4.3 (dual).

proof.text: The specified $E_D$ is exactly $K\times_{p,\mathcal C,q}A_D$: both conditions say that the target diagram is $p$ and every source vertex is in $D$. Pull back the inner-horn fillers and the horn-cocartesian lifts of step 1 along $p$. A horn problem over $K$ supplies its entire base simplex in advance; apply the filler in $A_D$ and pair it with that base simplex. The same argument applies to each defining outer-horn problem for a cocartesian edge, so its pullback remains cocartesian. This works for an arbitrary simplicial set $K$, without assuming it a quasicategory. The fiber over $v$ is $D\times_{\mathcal C,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,\mathcal C)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,\mathcal C}\{p(v)\}$, namely the arrow model of $D_{/p(v)}$. The lifts just constructed send $d\to p(v)$ to its composite $d\to p(v)\to p(w)$, with the composition homotopies supplied by the composition-spine theorem; these are the stated transport functors.

source.place: Base change of the cocartesian dual of Corollary 2.4.7.12; relative-slice construction used in Proposition 5.4.4.3.

proof.text: Write $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Fun}(K,\mathcal C)$ and $\mathcal B=\operatorname{Fun}(K,D)$. An $n$-simplex of the section simplicial set is a map $K\times\Delta^n\to E_D$ whose projection is $K\times\Delta^n\to K$. By the pullback definition and the exponential formula, this is precisely a map $d:K\times\Delta^n\to D$ and a map $H:K\times\Delta^n\times\Delta^1\to\mathcal C$ restricting to $d$ at $0$ and to $p\operatorname{pr}_K$ at $1$. Permuting the factors identifies these with the $n$-simplices of $T=\mathcal B\times_{\mathcal A,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,\mathcal A)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,\mathcal A}\{p\}$. This is a simplicial isomorphism: both faces and degeneracies are precomposition on $\Delta^n$. The arrow-target right-fibration theorem, applied to $\mathcal A$ and $p$, makes $T\to\mathcal B$ a right fibration by pullback. Since $\mathcal B$ is a quasicategory, its total space is a quasicategory (fill the base inner horn, then lift it). This proves the asserted coherent comma equivalence, including every higher simplex.

source.place: The section/comma identification in the relative-slice argument of Proposition 5.4.4.3; explicit exponential calculation, with Corollary 2.4.7.12 specialized to a fixed target.

proof.text: Suppose $D$ essentially small. Choose a small quasicategory $D_0$ and an equivalence $e:D_0\to D$ with quasi-inverse. Applying $\operatorname{Fun}(K,-)$ to the two functors and their inverse equivalences gives inverse functors between $\operatorname{Fun}(K,D_0)$ and $\mathcal B$. The whiskered equivalences are equivalences by the componentwise equivalence criterion. The former simplicial set is small: in degree $n$ its simplices are maps between the two small simplicial sets $K\times\Delta^n$ and $D_0$. Hence $\mathcal B$ is essentially small. In particular its diagrams $e d_0$, for vertices $d_0\in\operatorname{Fun}(K,D_0)$, form a small family of representatives up to equivalence.

source.place: Essential smallness of Fun(K,C^tau) in the proof of Proposition 5.4.4.3; expanded with a small model, without any compactness assumption.

proof.text: The local-smallness theorem for small functor shapes makes $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ locally small. Space-valued transport identifies the fiber of $T\to\mathcal B$ at $d$ with $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal A}(d,p)$, with precomposition as transport. For $(d,\alpha),(e,\beta)\in T$, the right-fibration morphism theorem therefore gives $\operatorname{Map}_T((d,\alpha),(e,\beta))\simeq\operatorname{hofib}_{\alpha}(\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal B}(d,e)\xrightarrow{h\mapsto\beta h}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal A}(d,p))$. This is essentially small: replace its two mapping spaces by small Kan models and use homotopy-pullback invariance; the path-space pullback of small models is small. Thus $T$ is locally small. For each representative $e d_0$ of step 4 choose a small Kan model of $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal A}(e d_0,p)$ and, for each of its vertices, a corresponding transformation. These choices form a small set of objects of $T$. Every $(d,\alpha)$ is equivalent to one of them: choose an equivalence $h:e d_0\to d$, form $\alpha h$, and choose a vertex in its component in the small mapping-space model. The square with components $h,1_p$ and its inverse square from $h^{-1},1_p$ exhibit an equivalence of pairs; the inverse witnesses are the whiskered inverse witnesses for $h$. A path from the chosen transformation to $\alpha h$ is an equivalence within the Kan fiber. Consequently the small family covers all objects of $T$ up to equivalence. Apply the small-full-subcategory theorem to this locally small $T$ and this family: its replete full span is all of $T$, proving essential smallness of the section category.

source.place: Agent size argument for the section category, using small mapping spaces and small representatives; compare the essential-smallness observation in Proposition 5.4.4.3. No compactness or filteredness is needed.

proof.text: Fix $x\in\mathcal C$ and model $\mathcal C_{/x}$ by the target-fixed arrow category. Its source projection is the right fibration classifying $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(-,x)$. For $a:A\to x$ and $b:B\to x$, the right-fibration morphism formula gives $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C_{/x}}(a,b)\simeq\operatorname{hofib}_{a}(\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)\xrightarrow{b\circ-}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(A,x))$. By exactly the degreewise exponential calculation of step 3, for every small simplicial set $J$ the category $\operatorname{Fun}(J,\mathcal C_{/x})$ is the target-fixed arrow category $\operatorname{Fun}(J,\mathcal C)_{/\Delta_Jx}$. Applying the same right-fibration formula in that quasicategory gives the corresponding formula for coherent transformations of $J$-diagrams over $x$, naturally in both diagrams. In particular it retains the homotopies imposing equality of their composites with the structure maps to $x$.

source.place: Mapping-space computation underlying Proposition 1.2.13.8, with the fixed-target arrow model; no assumption that C has all colimits.

proof.text: Let $q:J\to\mathcal C_{/x}$ have source diagram $a:J\to\mathcal C$, and let $\lambda:a\to\Delta_J L$ be any colimiting source cocone. We first construct a lift of this cocone. Use the join/fat-cone comparison to represent it by a colimiting diagram on $J^{\triangleright}$, with boundary fixed. Apply the parameter-cone-extension theorem with $B=\Delta^1$, $P=\partial\Delta^1$, and shape $J$. On $B\times J$ prescribe $q$, regarded as the transformation $a\to\Delta_Jx$. At vertex $0$ prescribe the source colimit cocone with apex $L$; at vertex $1$ prescribe the constant identity cocone with apex $x$. These prescriptions agree on $P\times J$. The only nondegenerate simplex of $B$ outside $P$ is the edge $0\to1$, whose initial vertex has precisely the colimit cocone $\lambda$. The theorem therefore extends them over $B\times J^{\triangleright}$, fixing the indicated union. It supplies an arrow $t:L\to x$ and a coherent cocone $q\to\Delta_Jt$ in $\mathcal C_{/x}$ with the prescribed source cocone. The join comparison transfers this construction back to the coherent-cocone model. This invocation requires only the colimit of $a$; the constant diagram at $x$ need not have a colimit equal to $x$.

source.place: Explicit extension version of the existence argument in Proposition 1.2.13.8; parameter-cone extension with P containing both vertices and the source endpoint colimiting.

proof.text: For every test arrow $b:B\to x$, compare the morphism formula of step 6 for $t$ with its diagram version for transformations $q\to\Delta_J b$. The two relevant maps are $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(L,B)\to\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(J,\mathcal C)}(a,\Delta_J B)$ and $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C}(L,x)\to\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(J,\mathcal C)}(a,\Delta_J x)$, each given by composition with $\lambda$. Both are equivalences by the dual cone criterion, since $\lambda$ is colimiting. They commute with postcomposition by $b$, and the lifted cocone identifies the image of $t$ with the transformation $a\to\Delta_Jx$ defining $q$. Homotopy-pullback invariance therefore identifies the homotopy fiber at $t$ of the first postcomposition map with the homotopy fiber at that transformation of the second. By step 6, this is exactly the equivalence $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal C_{/x}}(t,b)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(J,\mathcal C_{/x})}(q,\Delta_J b)$ induced by our cocone. The dual cone criterion in $\mathcal C_{/x}$ proves it colimiting. This argument works for every lift of a source colimit cocone. Conversely, since $a$ has a colimit, step 7 constructs one such colimiting lift; every other colimit of $q$ is equivalent to it, with its cocone, by contractibility of the space of colimiting cocones. Applying the source functor preserves this equivalence and the colimit property of its source cocone. Hence precisely the cocones with colimiting source are colimiting, under the stated existence hypothesis. This proves creation (up to its canonical contractible choice), preservation and detection for the colimits in question.

source.place: Agent mapping-space proof of the creation and characterization assertions of Proposition 1.2.13.8, using coherent natural-transformation fibers rather than a claim about Hom sets.

proof.text: Finally let the specified diagram shapes have colimits in $\mathcal C$ and let $D$ be closed under them. For any such diagram in $D_{/x}$ the source diagram lies in $D$, so its colimit $L$ in $\mathcal C$ lies in $D$. The lift constructed above is consequently an object of $D_{/x}$. This category is full in $\mathcal C_{/x}$, so the same equivalence on mapping spaces holds for every test object of $D_{/x}$ and makes this a colimit there. Any other colimit cocone in $D_{/x}$ is equivalent to it and therefore has the same source colimit property. For $f:x\to y$, postcomposition takes the colimit apex $t:L\to x$ to $ft:L\to y$ and leaves its source cocone unchanged. The characterization just proved for $D_{/y}$ makes the resulting cocone colimiting. Thus all the specified colimits are computed on sources and preserved by postcomposition. For the empty shape this says that an initial source $0\in D$ gives the initial arrow $0\to x$; the argument has used no nonemptiness of a shape.

source.place: Full-subcategory restriction and postcomposition consequence of Proposition 1.2.13.8; elementary conclusion from steps 6-8.
